sermon:
A man stands in a bookstore and runs his thumb down the spines, picking a teacher the way you pick a wine. Smooth. Confident. The one whose phrasing flatters the listener back to himself. This is older than the bookstore. In Corinth they were already doing it, dividing the church into fan clubs. I follow Paul. I follow Apollos. I follow Cephas. And Paul, who could have fought for his share of the market, instead burns the whole market down.

**The boast that splits a church**

The Corinthians thought they were arguing about teachers. Paul saw they were arguing about themselves. To attach your name to the most impressive voice is to borrow his weight, to stand a little taller in the crowd by association. So Paul asks the question that collapses the whole arrangement: 'Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?' (1 Corinthians 1:13). The answer is so obvious it shames the question. No one died for you in the bookstore. One man died for you, and his name is not on your faction's banner.

Underneath the parties was a hunger for eloquence, for wisdom that performs. Greece had taught these people to measure truth by how well it played in the room. And the gospel does not play well in that room. A Messiah nailed to a cross is, by every standard the room respects, a defeat. Paul does not apologize for this. He drives toward it.

**The wisdom that looks like failure**

'For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God' (1 Corinthians 1:18). Read that slowly. God chose the most humiliating instrument in the Roman world and made it the center of everything. Not despite its weakness. Because of its weakness. God chose what is foolish to shame the wise, what is weak to shame the strong, what is low and despised, even things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are. The logic is deliberate. He emptied the room of every boast before anyone could carry one in.

And then there is Paul himself, who came to them 'in weakness and in fear and much trembling,' whose speech was 'not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power' (1 Corinthians 2:4). The greatest mind in the early church showed up shaking, refusing to win them with technique, so that their faith would rest on God and not on a performance.

**What this asks of us**

I know this hunger because I have it. I have measured sermons by the response they got and not the cross they carried. I have wanted to be the smooth voice on the spine of the book. Every pastor who has ever counted his platform has stood with the Corinthians, dividing the body to feed his own name. The cross does not let us keep that. It says the smartest thing you ever said added nothing to your salvation, and the most embarrassing failure of your life did not subtract from it, because both were settled at a Roman execution you had no hand in.

This is the deepest mercy. If the gospel rested on eloquence, only the eloquent would be safe. If it rested on the cross, then the inarticulate, the slow, the unimpressive are as fully saved as Paul. Christ crucified is the great leveler. He took the lowest place so that no place is too low to be reached, and no height is high enough to need defending.

So lay the banner down. You did not earn the teacher you follow, and you cannot improve on the cross you were given. The boast you have been protecting was never going to hold your weight.

The cross ends our boasting.

Watch two toddlers in a nursery fight over a plastic toy that belongs to neither of them. The fierceness is total. The stakes are nothing. They will scream, claw, weep, all to claim a thing that was only ever on loan from the church basement. Paul looked at the Corinthians, so proud of their wisdom, and saw exactly this. Grown believers, fighting over field hands, on ground that was never theirs to claim.

**The proof of immaturity is the quarrel**

These were people who congratulated themselves on knowledge. Paul calls them infants. 'But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ' (1 Corinthians 3:1). And his evidence is not their theology. It is their behavior. 'For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh?' The proof of how grown you are is not what you know. It is whether you can stop fighting. A church can have impressive doctrine and the maturity of a nursery, and the quarreling is the tell. You cannot hide spiritual age. It shows up the moment someone disagrees with you.

The wisdom they boasted in was, Paul says, a borrowed thing they did not understand. The rulers of this age, with all their cleverness, crucified the Lord of glory because they could not see what the Spirit alone reveals. So the very wisdom the Corinthians used to rank their teachers was the wisdom that had killed Christ.

**The teachers are servants, the field is God's**

Then Paul does something to deflate the whole status game. He reduces the celebrities to laborers. 'I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth' (1 Corinthians 3:6-7). Picture the men you idolize as two hired hands at opposite ends of a field, sweating, and then picture the harvest belonging entirely to the owner. The argument over which servant is greater is an argument no servant would start. It is an argument the field-workers find embarrassing.

And the building they are working on is not a clubhouse for parties. 'Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you?' (1 Corinthians 3:16). This is the verdict that ends the fight. You are not a fan base divided among coaches. You are holy ground. The Spirit of God has taken up residence in this gathered people, and to split it into factions is to deface the temple. Paul's warning is severe: if anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him.

**Who this indicts**

I have been the toddler. I have defended my circle, my preferred voices, my corner of the church, as though the kingdom depended on my side winning. And every time I did, I was treating a servant as a savior and treating God's temple as my territory. We do this with denominations, with worship styles, with the famous names whose books line our shelves. We line up behind field hands and call it discernment.

The cure is to see whose temple this is. Christ did not die to start a debating society. He died to make a dwelling place for God out of quarreling people, and he is patient enough to keep building when we keep vandalizing. The same Lord the rulers crucified is the foundation no faction can lay again. 'For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ' (1 Corinthians 3:11). Build on him, and the parties lose their point. Everything already belongs to you, and you belong to Christ, and Christ to God.

So stop counting whose team is winning. The field is not yours. The harvest is not yours. The temple you keep dividing is the one place God chose to live.

You are God's temple, not factions.

There is a particular kind of letter you write to people who have started to embarrass themselves and do not know it yet. You cannot just scold them; pride deflects a scolding. So you hold up a mirror, and in the mirror you put yourself, beaten and ragged, and you let them see the gap between how they are living and how their fathers in the faith are dying. That is 1 Corinthians 4. The Corinthians thought they had arrived. Paul shows them what arrival actually costs.

**Stewards are judged by faithfulness, not applause**

Paul begins by refusing their verdict on him. They had been ranking him against Apollos, grading the apostles like contestants. He answers that he is a steward, and a steward answers to his master, not to the crowd. 'It is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy' (1 Corinthians 4:2). Then, astonishingly, he refuses even his own verdict on himself: 'I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me' (4:4). Here is a man who will not be flattered by their praise or destroyed by their criticism, because he has moved the court. The only opinion that finally lands is the one rendered when the Lord comes and discloses the purposes of the heart.

A church that lives for the crowd's verdict is a church that can be ruled by whoever shouts loudest. Paul has stepped out of that economy entirely.

**The kingdom is power, not talk**

Then the irony turns sharp. 'Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich. Without us you have become kings' (1 Corinthians 4:8). You can hear the ache under the sarcasm. These people felt finished, full, reigning, while the men who brought them the gospel were starving. So Paul lays the apostles' resume beside their fantasy: 'To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless... we have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things' (4:11-13). The word is garbage. The leftover after everything useful is taken. That is what the apostolic life looked like, while the church that received its gifts played at being kings.

And the verdict lands: 'For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power' (1 Corinthians 4:20). Not eloquence. Not the impressive gift displayed in the meeting. Power, the kind that endures hunger and homelessness without losing the gospel. A church can talk like kings and have no power at all.

**The question that stops the boast**

The sentence that cuts deepest is a question: 'What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?' (1 Corinthians 4:7). Every gift they were strutting over had been handed to them. The eloquence, the knowledge, the spiritual experience, all received, none earned. To boast in a gift is to forget the Giver and pretend you generated what you were given.

I feel the rebuke. I have boasted in gifts I did not make. I have wanted to reign now, full now, applauded now, while quietly skipping the part where the cross means a cruciform life. We want the kingdom without the garbage, the crown without the homelessness, the gift without the cross that made it ours. But the apostles imitated a Master who was himself made the refuse of the world, despised and rejected, that he might give us everything we now hold. Christ became scum so we could become kings. To boast as if we earned that is to spit at the cost.

So set down the things you have been carrying like trophies. They were placed in your hands. The God who gave them is the only one whose applause will still matter when the Lord comes and the hearts are disclosed.

Boast in nothing you received as gift.

A little yeast does not announce itself. You fold it into the dough and it disappears, and then quietly, invisibly, it works through the whole lump until everything is changed. The Corinthians were proud of a church that could tolerate anything. Paul tells them what their tolerance is doing in the dark. It is rising.

**The pride that protects sin**

There was a man in the church sleeping with his father's wife, a thing Paul says even the pagans did not stomach. And the church's response was not grief. 'And you are arrogant. Ought you not rather to mourn?' (1 Corinthians 5:2). This is the part we rush past. The sin was bad; the pride about the sin was the deeper sickness. They had mistaken their refusal to confront it for spiritual largeness. Look how loving we are. Look how we accept. Paul names it as boasting, and then he gives the line that exposes the whole logic: 'Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?' (5:6). Tolerated sin is never contained sin. It works through the body. So 'cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump' (5:7), and he grounds even this in Christ: 'For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.' The church is unleavened because the Lamb has already died. Purity is not how we earn him. It is how we stop contradicting him.

**The shame of the courtroom**

Then Paul turns to another scene. Believers were dragging each other before pagan judges, airing the family's disputes in front of the very world they would one day judge. 'To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong?' (1 Corinthians 6:7). Notice the standard. Winning the case is already losing. The question is not who is right in the dispute. The question is what the watching world learns about a people who cannot absorb a wrong for the sake of the Name. We were bought to be a colony of forgiveness, and we keep hiring lawyers.

**The body you do not own**

Last, the deepest of the three. The Corinthians had a slogan: all things are lawful. They used it to excuse sleeping with prostitutes, treating the body as a disposable wrapper around a soul that alone mattered. Paul will not let the body go. 'The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body' (1 Corinthians 6:13). Your body has a destiny. It will be raised. And right now it is a member of Christ and a temple of the Spirit. Then the verse that ends the argument: 'You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body' (6:19-20). There it is. The price was the blood of Christ. You were on the auction block of sin and he paid for you whole, body included, and now the body you treat as yours to spend is property bought at the cross.

**Where I stand in this**

I have done all three in miniature. I have called my cowardice tolerance and let the leaven rise. I have wanted to win the argument more than honor the Name. I have treated my body as mine to do with as I please, as though the resurrection were only about the soul. The cross says otherwise. The same Lamb whose death makes the church unleavened bought the body I keep pretending I own. Honoring God with the body is not legalism. It is the only honest response to a purchase already made.

So stop protecting the sin you have been proud of tolerating. Stop spending the body that is no longer yours. The price has been paid in full, and the receipt is a cross.

You were bought; honor God bodily.

Somebody in Corinth had written Paul a list of questions about sex and marriage, and you can almost feel the tension in the room as he answers. Half the church wanted to ban marriage as too worldly to be holy. The other half wanted to keep no boundaries at all. Paul refuses both fevers, and what he hands them instead is harder and freer than either: stay where grace found you, and there give yourself wholly to the Lord.

**Marriage is good, restraint is real**

Against the ascetics who thought celibacy made them spiritual, Paul affirms marriage and the duty husband and wife owe one another, refusing the idea that the body is too dirty for God. Against the libertines who thought any appetite could be indulged, he sets real limits. He does not pretend marriage is a lesser calling, nor that singleness is a deprivation. He treats both as gifts. 'Each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another' (1 Corinthians 7:7). This alone would heal half our debates. We tend to rank these states, to pity the single and crown the married, or to romanticize the single and burden the married. Paul ranks neither. He hands each its own grace and tells each to live in it.

**Stay where you were called**

The spine of the chapter is a single refrain. 'Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him' (1 Corinthians 7:17). He says it of the married and the single, the circumcised and the uncircumcised, the slave and the free. The point is not that change is forbidden. The point is that your station is not your problem. The Corinthians kept imagining holiness was somewhere other than where they stood, that if they could just rearrange their lives they would finally be devoted. Paul cuts the nerve of that restlessness. The Lord met you here. Be devoted here. Marriage will not make you holy and singleness will not make you holy; the Lord makes you holy, in the situation his grace found you.

He is honest about the cost on both sides. The married person is rightly anxious about pleasing a spouse; the single person is freed for 'undivided devotion to the Lord' (1 Corinthians 7:35). He is not shaming the married for their divided attention. He is naming reality so that no one stumbles into either state blind.

**The undivided heart**

Underneath every answer is one aim: an undivided heart. The reason Paul can sit so loosely to whether you marry is that neither marriage nor singleness is the point. The Lord is the point. 'The appointed time has grown very short... For the present form of this world is passing away' (1 Corinthians 7:29-31). A man who has seen the cross and the empty tomb cannot treat any earthly arrangement as final. They are real, they are good, and they are passing. Hold them with open hands.

I need this, because I am tempted to believe my devotion is being throttled by my circumstances. If I were single, I would pray more. If I were married, I would be steadier. If my house were quieter, my walk would be deeper. Paul calls this what it is: a way of postponing obedience by blaming my station. The Lord did not assign me a fantasy life to be faithful in. He assigned me this one. Christ himself was the most undivided man who ever lived, single, devoted, given wholly to his Father and poured out for a bride he was buying with his blood. His undivided heart is what purchased mine. Devotion is not waiting for better conditions. It is the offering of the life you actually have.

So stop rehearsing the holier version of yourself that lives in a different situation. He called you here. Give him your whole heart here.

Live for the Lord, undivided.

There is a kind of person who is always technically right and somehow leaves a wreckage behind him. He wins the argument and loses the room. The Corinthians had a whole class of these people, and they were proud of it. They knew their theology of idols was correct, and they used that correctness to walk over the consciences of weaker believers. Paul agrees with their doctrine and then tells them their doctrine, wielded that way, is a sin.

**Knowledge that wounds**

The issue was meat sacrificed to idols. The strong knew the truth: an idol is nothing, there is one God, the meat is just meat. Paul does not dispute the facts. He disputes what they are doing with the facts. 'This knowledge puffs up, but love builds up' (1 Corinthians 8:1). Two verbs, two architectures. Knowledge inflates the one who holds it; love constructs the one beside you. The Corinthians had chosen inflation. And the result was a weaker brother, watching the enlightened eat freely, being dragged back toward an idolatry he had barely escaped. Paul's verdict is staggering: 'And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died' (8:11). Christ died for that man. You were not willing to skip a meal for him. The cross sets the value of the brother, and our freedom keeps undervaluing what the cross priced so high.

**The apostle who surrendered his rights**

Then Paul does not just preach restraint; he models it, and the model is his whole apostleship. He had every right to be paid for his ministry, fed by the churches, accompanied by a wife. He proves the right at length from Scripture and common sense, and then he lays it down. 'But I have made no use of any of these rights' (1 Corinthians 9:15). He worked with his hands and preached for free, not because he had to, but so that nothing would obstruct the gospel for anyone. 'I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some' (9:22). This is not weakness; it is the discipline of an athlete. 'I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified' (9:27). The man telling them to surrender their rights had surrendered more than any of them, and he had done it on purpose.

**Whose rights are these**

Here is where it finds me. I am quick to know I am right and slow to ask whether being right is helping anyone. I have insisted on my freedom, my preference, my entitlement, and called it principle, while a weaker brother stumbled at the edge of my certainty. The question Paul presses is not whether I have the right. Usually I do. The question is what love does with a right. And love, when it looks at the brother for whom Christ died, lays the right down.

This is the pattern of the cross itself. Christ had every right, every prerogative of glory, and surrendered all of it to build us up at his own expense. He did not insist on what was his. He emptied himself for the weak, the wrong, the not-yet-saved. A church full of people defending their rights has forgotten the Lord who refused to defend his. Freedom that destroys a brother is not the freedom Christ purchased. He bought us free in order to make us servants of one another.

So before you exercise the right you are sure you have, look at the person it might wound. He cost the same blood you did.

Surrender your rights for love.

They had everything. The cloud over them by day, the sea split before them, water from the rock, bread from heaven. The generation that walked out of Egypt had more visible grace than any people before them, and their bodies fell scattered across the wilderness, a graveyard the length of a desert. Paul puts that graveyard in front of the overconfident Corinthians and says, plainly, this was written for you.

**Sacraments are not insurance**

The Corinthians thought their spiritual privileges made them safe. They had baptism, they had the Lord's table, surely they were beyond falling. Paul reaches back to Israel to break the spell. He even describes Israel in sacramental terms: 'all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink... and the Rock was Christ' (1 Corinthians 10:2-4). They had the signs. And 'with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness' (10:5). Then the warning every secure heart needs: 'Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall' (10:12). The privilege that does not produce obedience does not protect; it deepens the fall. The table is not a charm. It is a participation, and participation makes demands.

**You cannot share two tables**

This is the heart of it. The Corinthians wanted to keep one foot in the pagan feasts and one foot at the Lord's Supper, treating the idol meal as harmless since idols are nothing. Paul agrees the idol is nothing and then says something stands behind it. 'You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons' (1 Corinthians 10:21). The table is a covenant act. To eat is to belong. You cannot belong to Christ and to what crucified him at the same time. There is a jealousy in this Lord that the Corinthians had domesticated, and Paul will not let it stay tame. 'Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?' (10:22). The question answers itself.

**Freedom bent toward the other**

And yet Paul does not end in fear; he ends in love. Having warned against idolatry, he returns to the meat in the market and frees the conscience again: eat what is sold, raise no question. But the moment a brother's conscience is at stake, the freedom bends. The governing rule arrives: 'So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God' (1 Corinthians 10:31). Then the neighbor: 'not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved' (10:33). Liberty is real, and liberty is for the other. The same freedom that refuses the demon's table refuses also to wound the weak brother. Both are love.

I see my own presumption here. I have assumed that because I have the signs of grace I am safe to flirt with the things that destroy people. I have wanted both tables, the Lord's and the world's, and called it balance. And I have used my freedom for myself and called it maturity. The wilderness graveyard is a sermon to me. Those people had Christ as their Rock and still fell, because privilege without faithfulness is a tomb. The Lord who fed them from the rock is the Lord who feeds me from his own broken body, and that table will not share me with what killed him. He bought my whole allegiance. He means to have it.

So take heed where you stand, and bend your freedom toward the good of the one beside you.

Whatever you do, seek another's good.

Imagine a dinner where the host's friends eat steak and wine while his servants stand in the corner with empty hands, and everyone calls it a celebration of unity. That was the Lord's Supper in Corinth. The very meal meant to proclaim a body broken for all of them had become the place their divisions were most visible, the rich feasting while the poor went hungry. Paul says it bluntly: when you come together this way, 'it is not the Lord's supper that you eat' (1 Corinthians 11:20). You can hold the right ceremony and miss the whole thing.

**Worship that honors its order**

The chapter opens with a passage we argue over, about head coverings and the order of men and women in worship. Strip away the cultural particulars and the burden is this: how they presented themselves in worship either honored or dishonored the relationships God had woven into the gathering. Paul cares that worship not become a place where people seize glory for themselves or erase the distinctions God made. The Corinthians treated the assembly as a stage for self-display. Paul keeps pulling them back to honor, to mutual dependence: 'In the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman' (1 Corinthians 11:11). Worship is not where you assert yourself. It is where you take your honored place in a body you did not design.

**A table that exposes the heart**

Then the heavier matter. At the supper, 'one goes hungry, another gets drunk' (1 Corinthians 11:21). The meal that should erase the gap between rich and poor was advertising it. So Paul recites the words handed down to him, the oldest account of that night we possess: 'The Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, This is my body which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me' (1 Corinthians 11:23-24). That is what they were trivializing. A body broken for them, and they could not share their bread with a hungry brother at the very table that proclaimed it.

This is why Paul warns about eating 'in an unworthy manner' and being guilty of the body and blood. We have often read that as private introspection, a morbid checklist before communion. Read it in context. The unworthy manner is despising the poor at the table. 'Let a person examine himself' (11:28) means: look at how you are treating the body, both the bread and the brothers. 'For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself' (11:29). To fail to see the brother is to fail to see the Lord whose body makes you one.

**The discernment we lack**

I have come to the table thinking only of myself, my sin, my standing, and never once thought of the people beside me, whether I had wronged them, ignored them, eaten while they went without. Paul says that self is exactly the problem. The table that should humble the rich man and lift the poor one had been turned into another arena of status, and we still do it, every time we treat worship as a private transaction between me and God and never see the body I am bound to.

The cure is the body itself. Christ gave his body to make these unlikely people one, the rich and the poor, the strong and the weak, eating from one loaf to say they are one bread. To despise any member is to despise the Lord who died to gather them. He waited for us at this table when we deserved no place at it. We can wait for one another.

So when you come, look around before you look up. The body you are about to remember is also the body sitting next to you.

Discern the body at the table.

A hand cannot do what an eye does, and an eye is useless for gripping. Anyone can see this about a body. Somehow the Corinthians could not see it about the church. They had turned the gifts of the Spirit into a hierarchy, the showy gifts on top, the quiet ones beneath, and the members ranked accordingly. Paul takes the most ordinary fact in the world, that a body has many parts, and uses it to dismantle the whole pecking order.

**One Spirit, many gifts, common good**

First he kills the idea that the gifts are about the gifted. 'There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit' (1 Corinthians 12:4). The same Spirit, again and again, the same Lord, the same God working all of it. The variety is real, but the source is one, and the purpose is one: 'To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good' (12:7). Not for display. Not for status. For the common good. The gift in your hand was never given for you to admire. It was given for the body to use. The moment a gift becomes a trophy, it has been torn from its purpose. The Corinthians had a cabinet full of trophies and a church coming apart.

**The body cannot afford to lose a part**

Then the long, patient image of the body. The foot cannot quit because it is not a hand. The ear cannot resign because it is not an eye. 'If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing?' (1 Corinthians 12:17). A church of nothing but the impressive gift would be a monster, all eye, deaf and immobile. God deliberately made it otherwise. 'But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose' (12:18). Your place is not an accident you must apologize for. It is an arrangement God made.

And here Paul turns the hierarchy upside down. 'On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable' (1 Corinthians 12:22). The unseen organs keep you alive. The members the Corinthians ranked lowest are the ones the body cannot survive without. God gave greater honor to the part that lacked it, 'that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another' (12:25). The whole design is aimed at killing the division they were so proud of.

**Where pride hides**

I feel this in two directions, and both are sin. There is the eye that says to the hand, I have no need of you, the gifted believer who looks down on the unremarkable saint and cannot imagine the body needs him. And there is the foot that says, because I am not a hand, I do not belong, the quiet member who has decided his ordinary gift makes him expendable and so withdraws. Paul forbids both. The proud part and the despairing part are making the same mistake: judging worth by visibility. God does not measure that way. He arranged the weaker parts as indispensable on purpose.

The ground of all this is the body we were baptized into. 'For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body' (1 Corinthians 12:13). This is the body of Christ, formed by his death, animated by his Spirit, and he assigns every member his place. The hand does not earn its spot and the eye cannot lose its dependence. We are one because he made us one at the cross, and the Spirit who raised him distributes the gifts that hold us together. To rank the members is to second-guess the Lord who placed them.

So find your place and fill it, and honor the member the world overlooks. He is the one the body cannot live without.

The Spirit gifts for one body.

We have sentimentalized this chapter into a wedding decoration, embroidered it on pillows, read it over candlelight, and in doing so we have almost entirely missed why Paul wrote it. It is not a poem about romance. It is a rebuke to a church drunk on spiritual gifts, told that all their impressive abilities add up to nothing without the one thing they had neglected. Paul takes their entire trophy case and weighs it, and the scale reads zero.

**The arithmetic of nothing**

Listen to how relentless he is. 'If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing' (1 Corinthians 13:1-2). Tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith, the very gifts the Corinthians ranked highest, and Paul reduces each to nothing without love. Then he goes further than any of us would dare: 'If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing' (13:3). Sacrifice itself, even martyrdom, is empty without love. There is no spiritual achievement so high that love is optional. The achievement is the variable. Love is the constant. Take love out and the most dazzling Christian on earth is a clanging cymbal.

**Love is what it does**

Then Paul defines love, and notice he does it entirely in verbs. 'Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful' (1 Corinthians 13:4-5). Every line is an action, and almost every line is something a Corinthian was failing at. They were proud; love is not arrogant. They insisted on their rights; love does not insist on its own way. They quarreled; love is not irritable or resentful. This is not abstract. It is a mirror held up to a specific church doing specific damage, and it is a mirror held up to me. I can preach love and be impatient with the person in front of me. I can write about love and keep a record of who wronged me. The definition convicts because it is so concrete.

**The one thing that remains**

Finally Paul tells them why love outranks everything they prized: it is the only thing that lasts. 'Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away' (1 Corinthians 13:8). The gifts are scaffolding for a building under construction. When the building is finished, the scaffolding comes down. 'For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face' (13:12). The day is coming when prophecy is obsolete because the thing prophesied has arrived, when knowledge is swallowed by sight. On that day the impressive gifts will fall away like a child's toys, and love will still be standing, because love is the substance of the world to come.

Where did Paul learn this love that is patient, that does not insist on its own way, that bears all things and endures all things? He learned it at the cross. That is the only place this love has ever been fully spent. Christ was patient with us, kept no record of our wrongs, did not insist on his own way but gave up his body, not to be burned for nothing, but poured out in love that gains everything. The cross is 1 Corinthians 13 with skin on. We love because he first loved us like that.

So measure yourself by the only scale that survives the end of the world. Your gifts will pass. Your knowledge will pass. The question is whether you loved.

Without love you are nothing.

Picture a service where a dozen people are speaking at once, each in a language no one else understands, and a visitor wanders in off the street, listens for a moment, and concludes these people are out of their minds. That was a live possibility in Corinth. They had decided that the most ecstatic, least intelligible gift was the most spiritual, and Paul, who would not forbid tongues, spends a whole chapter pulling their worship back toward the one question they had stopped asking: did anyone leave built up?

**Worship is for building, not display**

Coming straight off the chapter on love, Paul applies it to the gathering. 'Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy' (1 Corinthians 14:1). Why prophecy over tongues? Not because tongues are bad, but because of who they serve. 'The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church' (14:4). There is the whole argument in one verse. The Corinthians prized the gift that fed the self. Paul prizes the gift that feeds the body. The standard for worship is not how spiritual it feels to me but whether it edifies the people around me. A gift that only lifts the one exercising it has, in the assembly, missed its point.

Paul drives it home with the picture of the outsider. If everyone speaks in tongues and a visitor walks in, 'will they not say that you are out of your minds?' (1 Corinthians 14:23). But if the word is intelligible and convicting, the outsider 'falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you' (14:25). Worship has a watching world at its edges. Intelligibility is not a concession to the weak; it is love reaching the outsider.

**Use the mind in worship**

The Corinthians had set the mind against the spirit, as though the more incomprehensible a thing was, the holier. Paul will not allow the split. 'I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also' (1 Corinthians 14:15). Then the verse that should be over the door of every gathering: 'In church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue' (14:19). Five understood words outweigh ten thousand ecstatic ones, because five words can build a brother and ten thousand cannot. God is not honored by spectacle that leaves the church no stronger.

**Order, because God is not confused**

So Paul gives practical order. Let two or three speak, one at a time. Let there be interpretation. Let it be weighed. And the reason underneath the rules is theological: 'For God is not a God of confusion but of peace' (1 Corinthians 14:33). The chaos in Corinth was not a sign of the Spirit's abundance. It was a contradiction of God's own character. The conclusion is calm and total: 'All things should be done decently and in order' (14:40).

I need this because I am tempted to measure worship by my own experience, by what stirred me, what felt powerful, and to forget the person in the next seat entirely. Paul says love asks a different question. Did the church get built? Did the outsider meet God? Was the body stronger when it walked out than when it walked in? Christ did not come to feed himself. He poured himself out to build a people, to make many members one body, and worship that serves only the worshiper has forgotten the Lord whose whole life was for others. The gathered church is his body, and the Spirit was given to build it.

So before you reach for what lifts you, ask what builds the room. Love sat down beside you, and love came to be understood.

In worship, build the church up.

Pull one thread and a sweater unravels in your hands. Some in Corinth had pulled a single thread, the resurrection of the dead, thinking they could remove just that one belief and keep the rest of the faith intact. Paul shows them what comes apart when it goes. Pull the resurrection and the whole gospel comes off the spool, and you are left holding a pile of loose string and calling it Christianity.

**Without the resurrection, nothing is left**

Paul starts with the gospel he received and passed on, the oldest creed in the New Testament: 'that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures' (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Then the witnesses, more than five hundred at once, most still alive to be questioned. This is not legend. It is testimony. Then he runs the terrible arithmetic of denial. 'If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain' (15:14). And worse: 'If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins' (15:17). The dead in Christ have simply perished. We are, of all people, most to be pitied. Paul will not let them keep a comfortable, resurrection-free religion. There is no such thing. Take the resurrection out and you do not have a gentler gospel; you have a corpse and a lie.

**Christ raised is the firstfruits**

But he turns. 'But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1 Corinthians 15:20). Firstfruits is the word that changes everything. The first sheaf of the harvest is the promise of the whole field. Christ's resurrection is not an isolated miracle; it is the opening of a harvest, and everyone in him is the rest of the crop. So death, which entered through one man, is undone through one man. 'For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive' (15:22). The grave is not the end of the story for anyone joined to the risen one. He went first so that we would follow.

**The body that will be raised**

Then Paul answers their real objection, which was probably disgust at the idea of the body returning. He does not promise a resuscitated corpse. He promises a transformed body, sown perishable and raised imperishable, sown in weakness and raised in power. 'For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality' (1 Corinthians 15:53). And then the taunt thrown at the grave itself: 'Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?' (15:54-55). The thing that has terrified every human being who ever lived is, in Christ, a defeated enemy with its teeth pulled.

Here is why this is not abstract. Paul ends not in the clouds but on Monday morning. 'Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain' (1 Corinthians 15:58). I have labored as though my work would be forgotten, served as though it would dissolve into nothing, grieved as though death had the last word over the people I have buried. The resurrection answers all of it. If Christ is risen, then nothing done for him is ever wasted. The visit no one saw, the prayer that seemed to change nothing, the faithfulness in a body that is failing, all of it is gathered into a harvest that death cannot touch. The empty tomb reaches forward and secures every act of love I thought would be lost.

So do not let anyone pull the thread. He is risen, and because he is, the grave is robbed and the work continues and nothing you give him falls to the ground.

Your labor is not in vain.

A great symphony does not end on its highest note. It comes down, gently, into the ordinary, resolving the enormous theme into something you can hum walking out the door. Paul has just thundered through the resurrection, the imperishable body, death swallowed in victory, and then the very next sentence is about a weekly offering. 'Now concerning the collection' (1 Corinthians 16:1). The largest truth in the universe lands on a question of money set aside on the first day of the week. That descent is the whole point. The resurrection is not meant to stay in the clouds. It comes down into the budget, the schedule, the love between people.

**The resurrection funds the collection**

The saints in Jerusalem were poor, and Paul was gathering relief for them across the Gentile churches. Notice how unspiritual the instructions sound. 'On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper' (1 Corinthians 16:2). Regular. Planned. Proportional. Everyone, not just the wealthy. This is generosity organized rather than emotional, the offering that comes from people who believe their labor is not in vain and so can let go of what they have. The chapter before promised an imperishable inheritance. This chapter spends present money on hungry brothers. That is exactly how resurrection hope is supposed to work. People sure of the harvest can afford to be openhanded now.

**Faithful labor, watchful love**

Then Paul turns to the work and the workers. He commends Timothy, urges them to honor those who labor, tells them to submit to such people and the fellow workers who toil alongside. And in the middle of these practical notes comes a string of commands that read like the whole Christian life compressed: 'Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love' (1 Corinthians 16:13-14). Watchfulness, steadiness, courage, strength, and then the word that governs all four. Love. After a letter spent correcting their arrogance, their lawsuits, their abuse of the table, their pride in gifts, it all comes down to this single instruction. Whatever you do, do it in love. Everything Paul has labored for in this letter fits inside that sentence.

**Longing for the Lord**

And then the ending leaves weight rather than resolving it. Paul writes a greeting in his own large hand, and lets fall a phrase in the old Aramaic of the first believers: 'Our Lord, come' (1 Corinthians 16:22). Maranatha. The hardest letter in his correspondence, full of rebuke, ends not with a tidy summary but with a cry of longing for the Lord to return. The man who has just defended the resurrection wants to see the risen one. He cannot fix this church completely; he can only love it and ache for the day when the Lord himself comes and finishes what no letter could.

I find myself indicted and comforted at once. I want my Christianity to stay at the level of the symphony's high note, the doctrine, the grand truth, and to skip the descent into the weekly offering, the unglamorous labor, the patient honoring of ordinary workers, the daily decision to do this particular thing in love rather than irritation. Paul will not let the gospel stay airborne. The same Lord who was raised commands the collection, the labor, the love, and the longing. He came down to us, into a body, into a death, into a grave, and out the other side, and a faith that refuses to come down into ordinary obedience has not understood him. He is coming again. Until then, every plain and unspectacular act is to be soaked in the one thing this letter has been after from the start.

So bring the great truth down into the room you actually live in. Set aside the gift, honor the worker, stand firm, and over all of it, love.

Let all you do be love.
